meta.title: Video Generation Concepts
meta.thesis: Video Generation Concepts is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A product marketer creates short demo clips and must control story, motion, consistency, and review. By the end, they should be able to build or review video-generation shot plan with prompt, reference, and QA notes, measure shots accepted without continuity errors, and catch the failure where each clip looks good alone but the product changes shape between shots.

mentalMap.title: Video Generation Concepts: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Understand video generation as image generation plus time: temporal consistency, conditioning, motion limits, review, and product caveats.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Video generation is hard because each frame must remain visually and semantically consistent over time.

blocks.title: A beautiful frame can make a bad video

spans.text: Problem anchor: a learning app wants a 4-second clip of a robot arranging concept cards. One frame looks great, but across frames the hand changes shape, cards flicker, labels mutate, and the camera jumps. Video generation must align appearance and motion over time.

blocks.analogy: Video generation is a flipbook where every page must remember the same world.

spans.text: The clip is rejected because concept-card labels mutate every half-second. The colors and style are good; the teaching signal is wrong.

blocks.title: Video challenge
blocks.prompt: What makes video harder than still images?

options.text: Objects, motion, and scene meaning must stay consistent across frames.
A video is one image with audio.

modules.title: Conditioning can start from text, image, or video
modules.sub: The input mode controls composition, identity, and rights risk.
modules.summary: Text-to-video, image-to-video, and control workflows offer different tradeoffs.

blocks.title: More conditioning usually means more control and more responsibility

spans.text: Text-to-video starts open-ended. Image-to-video starts from an approved frame and can preserve composition. Video-to-video or control-conditioned generation can preserve structure but inherits rights, privacy, and provenance questions from the source media.

modules.title: Short constrained motion beats long exact scenes
modules.summary: Generated video quality depends on motion priors, frame count, and reviewability.

blocks.title: The model must learn how things move

spans.text: Video models need motion patterns, not only appearance. Short clips with fixed camera and simple motion are easier to review than long scenes with multiple characters, exact text, and detailed procedures.
Good brief: 4 seconds, fixed camera, robot hand slides three blank concept cards into a row, no readable text. Risky brief: one-minute cinematic tutorial with exact labels and many characters.

modules.title: Code a temporal consistency check
modules.sub: Review adjacent frames, not only thumbnails.
modules.summary: A small report can flag flicker and jumps for human review.

blocks.title: Tiny frame-change report
blocks.code:
frames = [
    {"frame": 0, "brightness": 0.50, "card_x": 10},
    {"frame": 1, "brightness": 0.52, "card_x": 13},
    {"frame": 2, "brightness": 0.91, "card_x": 80},
    {"frame": 3, "brightness": 0.54, "card_x": 18},
]
alerts = []
for prev, cur in zip(frames, frames[1:]):
    if abs(cur["brightness"] - prev["brightness"]) > 0.25 or abs(cur["card_x"] - prev["card_x"]) > 25:
        alerts.append(cur["frame"])
print(alerts)

spans.text: Real systems can use optical flow, embeddings, or human review. The habit is to inspect continuity across frames.

predictThenReveal.answer: Frame 2, because brightness and position jump sharply from frame 1.

spans.text: Checklist: prompt/conditioning recorded; duration, fps, and resolution explicit; model/settings saved; review checks identity, motion, text artifacts, physics, and rights.

modules.title: Product caveats decide where video belongs
modules.sub: Motion can teach, distract, or mislead.
modules.summary: Generated video belongs where review and labeling can handle errors.

spans.text: Video feels real, so synthetic clips need labels, rights review, and content checks. Sometimes a still diagram, screen recording, or authored animation is safer than generated motion.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Use generated video when motion adds learning value and every frame can be reviewed.
blocks.useWhen: Use it for low-risk illustrative motion, mood clips, or drafts with synthetic labeling.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid factual procedures, identity-sensitive content, exact text, or rights-constrained media without review.

blocks.title: Format choice
blocks.prompt: When is a still diagram better than generated video?

options.text: When exact labels, measurements, or factual steps matter more than motion.
Only when file size is small.

blocks.explanation: Choose format by learning value and verification needs.

questions.q: What must remain consistent across frames for this clip to be usable?
questions.why: Video fails through flicker, identity drift, physics artifacts, and text mutation even when single frames look good.
questions.rot: Review motion, identity, scene continuity, duration, and rights.
